summary: Defines a socket as the unique identifier a message is sent to or from. It is a 32-bit number, with even numbers for receiving sockets and odd ones for sending. The note was written by Joel Winett of Lincoln Laboratory for the network socket committee.

eli5.summary: A socket is like a phone extension that picks one program among many on a computer. This note says how to number them.

how was a 32 bit socket divided

subtitle: How to carve a 32-bit socket number into home, user and tag fields so network use can be accounted for.

tldr.problem: Sockets needed a definition that identifies the process and user behind a connection, so that network usage can be logged meaningfully.
tldr.mechanism: A socket is a 32-bit number, with even numbers for receiving sockets and odd for sending. It splits into an 8-bit home field, a 16-bit user field and an 8-bit tag.
tldr.outcome: The scheme was implemented in the NCP on the Lincoln Laboratory 360/67 and allows 256 hosts and 65,536 users per host.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 147 as Unknown. It updates RFC 129 and has no obsoleting or updating RFCs.

sections.title: What a Socket Is
sections.content:
A socket is the unique identification to or from which information is transmitted in the network. It is a 32 bit number: even sockets identify receiving sockets and odd sockets identify sending sockets. A socket is also identified by the host where the sending or receiving process runs.

Earlier papers described processes with access to a number of ports, such as a physical device or a logical I/O device. A socket is the identification of a port for machine to machine communication through the ARPA network. Communication is always from one socket to another, each tied to a process at a known host.
sections.eli5: A socket is a numbered mailbox. Odd numbers are for sending, even numbers are for receiving, and each one belongs to a program on a certain computer.

sections.title: Well-Known and Negotiated Sockets
sections.content:
Sockets allocated to each host must be uniquely associated with a known process or be undefined. The names of some sockets must be universally known and tied to a process using a specified protocol, for example a logger socket, an RJE socket or a file transfer socket. Other socket names are not universal but are given in a transmission over a well-known socket, such as the socket pair named over the logger socket under the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP).

The note raises open questions: must users know socket names, or can this be transparent? Should a process reuse the same socket later for the same purpose? If sockets are visible to users, they must not depend on the order in which connections are made.
sections.eli5: Some mailboxes have famous numbers everyone knows. For others, you get the number in a message sent to a famous one.

sections.title: The Suggested Socket Layout
sections.content:
For accounting, the NCPs should log each connection with its start and close times, the number of messages and bits, the hosts and the sockets used. For those sockets to be meaningful they should identify the user, account or process. The note suggests dividing the 32 bit socket into an 8 bit home field, a 16 bit user field and an 8 bit tag. The tag is a 7 bit plug and a one bit polarity, where 0 means receive and 1 means send.

This gives a user up to 128 send sockets and 128 receive sockets, and allows 256 hosts and 65,536 users per host. The hard part is mapping a process identifier to a 16 bit user number, for example by table lookup, possibly with hash coding. A run time process index is no good because it differs between runs.

The logger socket at the Lincoln Laboratory 360/67 is given as x'0A000001': home 10, user 0, tag 1.
sections.eli5: Think of a long phone number split into three parts: which building, which person, and which line, with the last digit saying listening or talking.

fields.name: User
fields.desc: Identifies the user; allows 65,536 users per host.

fields.name: Plug
fields.desc: Part of the tag; up to 128 sockets per direction.

fields.name: Polarity
fields.desc: 0 for a receive socket, 1 for a send socket.
